lessons.title: Hello, World
intro: 1983: Borland sells Turbo Pascal for $49.95. It compiles in seconds on an IBM PC, and a whole generation learns to program with it. The language itself is older: Niklaus Wirth designed Pascal in 1970 in Zurich, to teach programming the clean way.
A Pascal program starts with program and a name. The statements go between begin and end, and the very last end has a full stop: end.
writeln('…') prints the text between the single quotes, and then moves to the next line.

options: Prints text and then moves to a new line

exercises.prompt: How does the last line of every Pascal program look?
exercises.explanation: The final end has a full stop. All the others don't.
The program ends with end and a full stop.

exercises.prompt: Which quotes does Pascal use for text?

exercises.explanation: Each writeln prints its text and moves to the next line.
Wirth named it after the 17th-century mathematician Blaise Pascal, who built one of the first mechanical calculators.

lessons.title: write and writeln
intro: write prints without moving to a new line, so the next output continues on the same line. writeln prints and then starts a new line. An empty writeln just makes a blank line.
One writeln can print several things, separated by commas: writeln('Answer: ', 42).
Numbers are written without quotes, and Pascal can calculate: writeln(6 * 7) prints 42.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between write and writeln?
options: writeln moves to a new line afterwards, write doesn't
exercises.explanation: write keeps the cursor on the same line.
Three writes all stay on one line, and the final writeln ends it.
The text in quotes is printed as it is; the calculation outside the quotes is worked out.
writeln with nothing to print makes a blank line.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order to print Hello, Pascal! on one line.
exercises.explanation: write first, so writeln can continue on the same line.
The ' ' between the numbers prints a space.

lessons.title: Semicolons and Comments
intro: In Pascal, ; separates statements, like commas in a list. That's why the statement right before end doesn't need one (but one there doesn't hurt). A missing ; between two statements is the most common error: Turbo Pascal stops with Error 85: ";" expected.
Comments are notes for people: everything between { and } is ignored. (* and *) work too.
Pascal doesn't care about upper and lower case: WriteLn, WRITELN and writeln are the same.

code: { This program prints a short poem }
WRITELN('Pascal is blue,');  (* case doesn't matter *)

options: A semicolon is missing between two statements
There is a spelling mistake in writeln
exercises.explanation: Turbo Pascal shows it at the end of the line where the ; should be.

exercises.prompt: This program doesn't compile. Which line is missing a semicolon?
exercises.explanation: Between the two writelns there must be a ;.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a comment in Pascal?
exercises.explanation: Curly brackets (and (* *)) mark comments. Newer Pascals also allow //.

exercises.prompt: Are writeln and WriteLn the same in Pascal?
options: Yes, Pascal ignores upper and lower case
exercises.explanation: Unlike C, Pascal is not case-sensitive.

exercises.prompt: Does the statement right before end need a semicolon?
options: No, ; only separates statements, but one there is allowed
No, and one there is an error
